subject: Biology
title: Biotechnology and its Applications
summary: The chapter takes the tools of Chapter 9 (restriction enzymes, vectors, PCR, cloning) and shows what they have actually produced: Bt cotton and RNAi-protected tobacco in agriculture; recombinant human insulin, gene therapy for ADA deficiency and PCR/ELISA-based early diagnosis in medicine; transgenic animals such as the cow Rosie; and the ethical machinery of GEAC, patents and biopiracy. It is short, fact-dense and asked every year, so it repays exact names, dates and sequences.

exam_profile.weightage: Class 12 Biology theory is a 70-mark paper. This chapter belongs to the Biotechnology unit, which in the current CBSE scheme typically carries about 10 marks together with Chapter 9 (Biotechnology: Principles and Processes). Chapter 10 typically contributes 5 to 7 of those marks: one or two 1-mark items, a 2-mark question, and a 3-mark or 5-mark question on Bt cotton, RNAi, insulin or gene therapy, with the Bt cotton or ADA gene therapy story appearing as a case-based question in some years.

question_types.note: Which cry gene controls which pest, the year and patient of the first gene therapy, what the C-peptide is, the source organism of the Bt toxin, which insect orders Bt kills, the vector used for RNAi in tobacco and for ADA cDNA, the percentage of transgenic animals that are mice, what Rosie's milk contained, the full form of GEAC, the year of the Basmati patent.

Bt toxin does not kill Bacillus thuringiensis because it exists as an inactive protoxin; ERT for ADA is not curative; recombinant insulin does not cause allergy because it is a human protein; dsRNA silences mRNA; PCR detects a pathogen before symptoms appear; transgenic mice used for vaccine safety; biopiracy and traditional knowledge.

Name the two cry genes for bollworm; what change pro-insulin undergoes; why animal insulin was replaced; two treatments for ADA deficiency and why they are not curative; how dsRNA enters a cell; what a probe is; two uses of transgenic animals; two objectives of GEAC; what biopiracy is.

Why lepidopterans die on Bt cotton (the full protoxin-to-lysis sequence); the RNAi strategy against Meloidogyne incognita in correct sequence; how Eli Lilly made insulin and how it differs from pancreatic insulin; gene therapy for ADA deficiency and why it needs periodic infusion; why molecular diagnosis is preferred, with PCR and ELISA; three arguments for GM crops; three uses of transgenic animals with examples.

Bt cotton from Bacillus thuringiensis to the dead bollworm, with a labelled flow diagram; RNAi from Agrobacterium to the dead nematode; the complete insulin story (animal insulin, its problems, pro-insulin, the C-peptide, Eli Lilly's method); gene therapy with the ADA example and the permanent cure; the five uses of transgenic animals; ethical issues, GEAC, the Basmati case and biopiracy.

A passage on Bt cotton or a farmer's field with questions on the cry genes, the protoxin and insect specificity; a passage on a child with ADA deficiency asking about the enzyme, the vector, the cells used and why the cure is not permanent; a passage on Rosie or on the Basmati patent.

sections.heading: Introduction: what biotechnology now delivers, and the three areas of research
sections.body:
Chapter 9 gave you the tool kit: restriction enzymes, vectors, competent hosts, PCR, bioreactors and downstream processing. This chapter answers the question every student should ask at the end of that one: what has all this actually produced? NCERT's answer is that biotechnology deals with the industrial-scale production of biopharmaceuticals and biologicals using genetically modified microbes, fungi, plants and animals. The applications it lists are worth remembering as a set, because a 1-mark question can ask for any four of them: therapeutics, diagnostics, genetically modified crops for agriculture, processed food, bioremediation, waste treatment and energy production.

NCERT also names three critical research areas on which all of this rests, and they turn up as a 3-mark question more often than you would expect:

  1. Providing the best catalyst in the form of an improved organism, usually a microbe, or a pure enzyme.
  2. Creating optimal conditions through engineering for that catalyst to act.
  3. Downstream processing technologies to purify the protein or organic compound.

Keep the order and the wording; the examiner is looking for the words catalyst, optimal conditions and downstream processing.

The chapter then walks through four fields in a fixed order, and that order is how you should revise it: agriculture (10.1), medicine (10.2), transgenic animals (10.3) and ethical issues (10.4). Within agriculture there are two worked examples, Bt cotton and RNAi-protected tobacco. Within medicine there are three, genetically engineered insulin, gene therapy for ADA deficiency and molecular diagnosis. Almost every board question from this chapter is one of these five stories told in full, or a single fact pulled out of one of them. If you can narrate each story in the right sequence with the right names, the chapter is done.

One more thing about the CBSE syllabus line for this chapter: it lists human insulin and vaccine production, stem cell technology, gene therapy, Bt crops, transgenic animals, biosafety, biopiracy and patents. The NCERT text does not have a separate section on stem cells or vaccines, so questions on those stay at the level of a sentence: the hepatitis B vaccine is made in yeast by rDNA technology (you met this in Chapter 7), and stem cells are unspecialised cells that can be coaxed to form the cell types a patient has lost.
sections.tip: If a question asks for 'areas of application of biotechnology', give the NCERT list verbatim. If it asks for 'critical research areas', give the three-point list about catalyst, conditions and downstream processing; these are two different questions and students mix them up.

sections.heading: 10.1 Biotechnological Applications in Agriculture: the three options and what GM plants offer
sections.body:
NCERT opens the agriculture section with a choice. To increase food production there are three options: agro-chemical based agriculture, organic agriculture, and genetically engineered crop-based agriculture. The Green Revolution succeeded in tripling the food supply, but that is still not enough to feed the growing human population, and its gains came only partly from improved crop varieties; mainly they came from better management practices and the use of agrochemicals (fertilisers and pesticides). Two problems follow. Agrochemicals are often too expensive for farmers in the developing world, and conventional breeding cannot push yields any further. That is the case for the third option.

A genetically modified organism (GMO) is a plant, bacterium, fungus or animal whose genes have been altered by manipulation. This is the definition the examiner wants for 'What is a GMO?'. NCERT then gives the list of what genetic modification has done for plants, and this list is asked directly as 'advantages of GM crops' or 'arguments in favour of GM crops':

  1. Made crops more tolerant to abiotic stresses: cold, drought, salt, heat.
  2. Reduced reliance on chemical pesticides, through pest-resistant crops.
  3. Helped to reduce post-harvest losses.
  4. Increased the efficiency of mineral usage by plants, which prevents early exhaustion of soil fertility.
  5. Enhanced the nutritional value of food, for example vitamin A-enriched rice (golden rice).

NCERT adds a sixth use in the same paragraph: GM has been used to create tailor-made plants that supply alternative resources to industries in the form of starches, fuels and pharmaceuticals. A 5-mark question on 'potential applications of GM plants' should include this along with the five above.

The disadvantages are not spelt out in this section but they are asked (NCERT exercise 3 says 'compare and contrast'). Draw them from the ethics section and general knowledge: unpredictable effects when a GMO enters an ecosystem, gene flow to wild relatives, possible allergenicity of the new protein, evolution of resistance in the target pest, loss of biodiversity if a few GM varieties dominate, dependence of farmers on seed companies, and patent disputes.
sections.tip: When asked for advantages of GM crops, write the five NCERT points as five separate lines with a keyword each (stress tolerance, less pesticide, less post-harvest loss, mineral efficiency, nutrition). One paragraph that mentions three of them earns three marks out of five at best.

sections.heading: 10.1 Bt cotton: Bacillus thuringiensis, the crystal protein and the cry genes
sections.body:
This is the most-asked story in the chapter. Tell it in this order.

The bacterium. Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt for short) is a soil bacterium that produces proteins that kill certain insects: lepidopterans (tobacco budworm, armyworm), coleopterans (beetles) and dipterans (flies, mosquitoes). During a particular phase of its growth the bacterium forms protein crystals, and these crystals contain a toxic insecticidal protein.

Why the bacterium is not killed by its own toxin. The Bt toxin exists inside the bacterium as an inactive protoxin. Nothing happens until an insect ingests it. In the insect's gut the alkaline pH solubilises the crystals and converts the protoxin into the active toxin. The activated toxin binds to the surface of the midgut epithelial cells and creates pores. The cells swell and lyse, and the insect dies. Marking schemes for 'why do lepidopterans die on Bt cotton' reward exactly these steps: ingestion, alkaline gut, activation, binding to midgut epithelium, pores, swelling and lysis, death.

The genes. Specific Bt toxin genes were isolated from Bacillus thuringiensis and incorporated into several crop plants such as cotton. The genes are named cry (from crystal), and there are many of them. The choice of gene depends on the crop and the target pest, because most Bt toxins are insect-group specific. Learn three: proteins coded by cryIAc and cryIIAb control the cotton bollworm; the protein coded by cryIAb controls the corn borer. The 2019 board paper asked for the two bollworm genes as a 1-mark question, and students who wrote cryIAb lost the mark.

What the plant then does. A Bt cotton plant carries the cry gene and therefore makes the crystal protein in its own tissues. A bollworm larva that bites the boll eats the protoxin, its alkaline gut activates it, and it dies. NCERT's Figure 10.1 contrasts a cotton boll destroyed by bollworms with a fully mature, healthy boll; the point of the figure is that the transgenic plant no longer needs chemical insecticide against that pest.

Two naming details that cost marks: the gene is written in lower-case italics, cry, and the protein is Cry with a capital C. Also, Bt toxin is a protein, not a chemical insecticide, and it is specific, so it does not harm insects that lack the alkaline gut and the receptors.
sections.tip: Write the gene names exactly: cryIAc and cryIIAb for bollworm, cryIAb for corn borer. Examiners compare letter by letter; cryIAc and cryIAb differ by a single letter and control different pests.

sections.heading: 10.1 Pest-resistant plants: RNA interference against the nematode Meloidogyne incognita
sections.body:
The second agricultural story is about a worm, not an insect. Several nematodes parasitise a wide variety of plants and animals, humans included. One of them, Meloidogyne incognita (NCERT prints it as Meloidegyne incognitia; either spelling is accepted), infects the roots of tobacco plants and causes a large reduction in yield. The strategy used against it is based on RNA interference (RNAi).

What RNAi is. RNAi takes place in all eukaryotic organisms as a method of cellular defence. It involves silencing of a specific mRNA by a complementary double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) that binds to the mRNA and prevents its translation. That is the whole definition and it is the 2-mark answer to 'What is RNAi?'. Where does a cell naturally get such complementary RNA? NCERT gives two sources: an infection by viruses with RNA genomes, or mobile genetic elements (transposons) that replicate through an RNA intermediate. 'How does dsRNA gain entry into a eukaryotic cell?' has been asked in exactly these words.

The strategy, in sequence. (1) Nematode-specific genes were introduced into the host tobacco plant using Agrobacterium vectors. (2) The DNA was introduced in such a way that it produced both sense and antisense RNA in the host cells. (3) These two RNAs, being complementary, base-paired to form dsRNA. (4) The dsRNA initiated RNAi and silenced the specific mRNA of the nematode. (5) The parasite, unable to make that essential protein, could not survive in a transgenic host expressing the interfering RNA, so the plant protected itself. The 2018 paper asked for this 'in correct sequence', which tells you what the marking scheme looks like: one mark for each numbered step, and steps out of order lose marks.

NCERT's Figure 10.2 shows three root systems side by side: (a) the roots of a typical healthy plant, (b) the roots of a nematode-infested plant, with knots and stunted growth, and (c) the roots of the transgenic plant, healthy again. If you are asked to draw it, three simple root sketches with those three captions are enough.

Notice the logic that links this to Bt cotton. In both cases the plant is given a gene and makes a product in its own tissues; in Bt the product is a protein that kills the pest, in RNAi the product is an RNA that switches off a gene in the pest. Questions often ask you to name 'the strategy' (RNAi) and 'the vector' (Agrobacterium) separately, so keep both words ready.
sections.tip: Three names, no more: the pest is Meloidogyne incognita, the host is tobacco roots, the vector is Agrobacterium. Students write 'E. coli' for the vector out of habit and lose the mark; plants are transformed with Agrobacterium.

sections.heading: 10.2 Biotechnological Applications in Medicine: recombinant therapeutics
sections.body:
The medicine section begins with a claim that is worth quoting in an answer: recombinant DNA technology has had an immense impact on healthcare by enabling the mass production of safe and more effective therapeutic drugs. The important adjective is safe. Recombinant therapeutics do not induce unwanted immunological responses, which is common when the same product is isolated from a non-human source. This one sentence is the reason recombinant insulin replaced animal insulin, and it is the reason recombinant human growth hormone replaced hormone extracted from cadaver pituitaries; keep it in mind for every question on 'why recombinant?'.

NCERT gives two numbers and both have been asked as 1-mark fill-ups: at present about 30 recombinant therapeutics have been approved for human use the world over, and in India 12 of these are being marketed. Recombinant products in this category include insulin, growth hormone, erythropoietin, interferons, clotting factor VIII and the hepatitis B vaccine; NCERT names only insulin in detail, so the others are for context and for the 'vaccine production' line of the syllabus.

The section then breaks into three subsections, and you should be able to say in one line what each is about before you learn the details:

  • 10.2.1 Genetically engineered insulin: how a human hormone is made in a bacterium and why the pro-hormone structure was the hard part.
  • 10.2.2 Gene therapy: how a missing gene can be supplied to a patient's cells, with ADA deficiency as the first clinical case.
  • 10.2.3 Molecular diagnosis: how PCR, DNA probes and ELISA detect a disease before symptoms appear.

A common 3-mark question strings these together: 'Mention three applications of biotechnology in medicine, with one example each.' The answer is therapeutics (recombinant insulin), gene therapy (ADA deficiency) and diagnostics (PCR for HIV, ELISA). Add the hepatitis B vaccine from yeast if a fourth is asked. The next three sections give each story in full.
sections.tip: The phrase the examiner is looking for in 'why recombinant therapeutics are preferred' is 'do not induce unwanted immunological responses'. Write it in those words.

sections.heading: 10.2.1 Genetically engineered insulin
sections.body:
The problem. Adult-onset diabetes can be managed by taking insulin at regular intervals. Insulin was earlier extracted from the pancreas of slaughtered cattle and pigs. This animal insulin worked, but it caused some patients to develop allergy or other reactions to the foreign protein. That is the 2-mark answer to 'why is animal insulin no longer used'; a slaughter-based supply also could not keep pace with demand, which you may add.

The structure. Insulin consists of two short polypeptide chains, chain A and chain B, linked together by disulphide bridges. (Chain A has 21 amino acids and chain B has 30; NCERT does not give the numbers but they help you draw the figure to scale.) In mammals, including humans, insulin is synthesised as a pro-hormone, which, like a pro-enzyme, must be processed before it becomes a fully mature and functional hormone. Pro-insulin contains an extra stretch called the C peptide that connects chain A to chain B. The C peptide is not present in mature insulin; it is removed during maturation. So the 'chemical change that pro-insulin undergoes to become mature insulin' (asked in 2018) is the removal of the C peptide, and the 'role of the C peptide' (asked in 2014) is that it holds the A and B chains together in the pro-hormone and is cut out on maturation.

The challenge. A bacterium has no machinery to cut the C peptide out of pro-insulin. So the main challenge in making insulin by rDNA technology was getting insulin assembled into its mature form.

The solution. In 1983, Eli Lilly, an American company, prepared two DNA sequences corresponding to the A and B chains of human insulin and introduced them into plasmids of E. coli to produce the insulin chains. Chains A and B were produced separately, extracted, and combined by creating disulphide bonds to form human insulin. The company went round the C-peptide problem by never making pro-insulin at all. This recombinant insulin, sold as humulin, is identical to the human hormone and does not provoke the reactions that animal insulin did.

The difference examiners ask for. Insulin made by the human pancreas is first synthesised as pro-insulin with three parts (A, B and C peptide) and matured by removing C. Insulin made by Eli Lilly is assembled directly from separately made A and B chains; no C peptide is ever involved. Write both halves of this contrast for a 2-mark 'how does it differ' question.

NCERT's Figure 10.3, 'maturation of pro-insulin into insulin (simplified)', is a frequent diagram question and is described in the diagrams section below.
sections.tip: Four facts get the 3 marks on the Eli Lilly question: 1983; two DNA sequences for chains A and B; plasmids of E. coli; chains produced separately, extracted and joined by disulphide bonds. Miss the word 'separately' and you have missed the point of the method.

sections.heading: 10.2.2 Gene therapy: the ADA deficiency example
sections.body:
Definition. Gene therapy is a collection of methods that allows correction of a gene defect that has been diagnosed in a child or embryo. Genes are inserted into a person's cells and tissues to treat a disease. The correction involves the delivery of a normal gene into the individual or embryo to take over the function of, and compensate for, the non-functional gene. Write the definition with the word 'compensate'; that is NCERT's key idea. The defective gene is not repaired or removed, it is supplemented.

The first case. The first clinical gene therapy was given in 1990 to a 4-year-old girl with adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency. ADA is an enzyme crucial for the immune system to function; without it lymphocytes cannot survive and the child has severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID). The disorder is caused by the deletion of the gene for adenosine deaminase. When asked 'the cause and the body system affected', the answer is gene deletion and the immune system.

Two conventional treatments, and why neither is enough. In some children ADA deficiency can be cured by bone marrow transplantation. In others it can be treated by enzyme replacement therapy (ERT), in which functional ADA is given to the patient by injection. The problem with both approaches is that they are not completely curative: a matched donor is not always available, and injected enzyme is used up, so the injections must be repeated for life. The 2016 paper asked for ERT and two of its disadvantages, and the marking scheme wanted 'not completely curative' and 'requires periodic injections'.

The gene therapy protocol, in sequence. (1) Lymphocytes from the patient's blood are grown in culture outside the body. (2) A functional ADA cDNA is introduced into these lymphocytes using a retroviral vector. (3) The engineered lymphocytes are returned to the patient. (4) Because lymphocytes are not immortal, the patient needs periodic infusion of such genetically engineered lymphocytes. Note two things students get wrong: it is cDNA (made from ADA mRNA by reverse transcriptase, so it has no introns and can be expressed in the target cell) and the vector is a retrovirus, not a plasmid.

The permanent cure. If the gene isolated from marrow cells producing ADA is introduced into cells at an early embryonic stage, it could be a permanent cure, because every cell of the body, including the stem cells that keep producing lymphocytes, would then carry the working gene. This is the standard 1-mark 'suggest a permanent cure' answer.
sections.tip: Lymphocytes, retroviral vector, ADA cDNA, periodic infusion, embryonic stage for a permanent cure: five keywords, five marks. Students who write 'bone marrow cells are given the gene' describe the permanent cure, not the 1990 therapy, and lose the sequence marks.

sections.heading: 10.2.3 Molecular diagnosis: PCR, DNA probes and ELISA
sections.body:
Why it matters. For effective treatment of a disease, early diagnosis and an understanding of its pathophysiology are very important. Conventional methods (serum and urine analysis and the like) cannot detect a disease early, because the presence of a pathogen is normally suspected only when it has already produced a symptom, and by then its concentration in the body is already very high. Three techniques serve the purpose of early diagnosis: recombinant DNA technology, PCR and ELISA. 'Why is molecular diagnosis preferred over conventional methods?' (asked in 2016) wants exactly this: early detection, before symptoms, when pathogen numbers are still very low.

PCR. A very low concentration of a bacterium or virus, at a time when symptoms are not yet visible, can be detected by amplification of its nucleic acid by PCR. PCR is now routinely used to detect HIV in suspected AIDS patients. It is also used to detect mutations in genes in suspected cancer patients, and it is a powerful technique for identifying many other genetic disorders. Give both examples, HIV and cancer, when asked for the uses of PCR in diagnosis.

The radioactive probe. A single-stranded DNA or RNA tagged with a radioactive molecule is called a probe. It is allowed to hybridise to its complementary DNA in a clone of cells, and the result is read by autoradiography. The logic of detecting a mutation is the part students must state clearly: the probe is made complementary to the normal gene, so the clone carrying the mutated gene does not appear on the photographic film, because the probe has no complementarity with the mutated sequence and does not bind. Normal cells light up; mutant cells stay dark.

ELISA. The Enzyme-Linked Immuno-Sorbent Assay is based on the principle of antigen–antibody interaction. Infection by a pathogen can be detected in two ways: by the presence of antigens (proteins, glycoproteins and so on) of the pathogen, or by detecting the antibodies that the body has synthesised against the pathogen. In Chapter 7 you learnt that ELISA is the usual screening test for HIV, and the two chapters are often linked in one question: PCR detects the viral nucleic acid, ELISA detects the viral antigen or the antibody to it.

A neat way to keep the three straight for a 3-mark question: PCR detects the pathogen's nucleic acid; a probe detects a specific gene sequence (normal versus mutant); ELISA detects a protein (antigen or antibody). One line each with an example, and the marks are yours.
sections.tip: For the probe question, the sentence that earns the mark is 'the clone with the mutated gene will not appear on the film because the probe is not complementary to it'. Students often write the opposite, that the mutant lights up.

sections.heading: 10.3 Transgenic Animals
sections.body:
Definition. Animals that have had their DNA manipulated to possess and express an extra (foreign) gene are known as transgenic animals. Transgenic rats, rabbits, pigs, sheep, cows and fish have been produced, although over 95 per cent of all existing transgenic animals are mice. The definition and the 95 per cent figure are both 1-mark regulars.

NCERT asks why such animals are made and gives five purposes. Learn the heading of each, then one example under it; a 5-mark question wants all five, a 3-mark question wants any three with examples.

  1. Normal physiology and development. Transgenic animals are designed to allow the study of how genes are regulated and how they affect the normal functions of the body and its development. NCERT's example is the insulin-like growth factor: by introducing genes that alter its formation and studying the biological effects, we learn about the biological role of the factor.
  2. Study of disease. Many transgenic animals are designed to increase our understanding of how genes contribute to the development of disease. They serve as models for human diseases so that new treatments can be investigated. Transgenic models exist for cancer, cystic fibrosis, rheumatoid arthritis and Alzheimer's.
  3. Biological products. Medicines for certain human diseases contain biological products that are expensive to make. A transgenic animal that produces a useful product can be created by introducing the DNA (gene) that codes for it. The example is the human protein α-1-antitrypsin, used to treat emphysema; similar attempts are being made for phenylketonuria (PKU) and cystic fibrosis. In 1997 the first transgenic cow, Rosie, produced human protein-enriched milk (2.4 grams per litre). The milk contained human α-lactalbumin and was a nutritionally more balanced product for human babies than natural cow milk. 'How is Rosie different from a normal cow?' has been asked twice; the answer is the α-lactalbumin, the quantity and the reason it matters.
  4. Vaccine safety. Transgenic mice are being developed to test the safety of vaccines before they are used on humans, and are already being used to test the safety of the polio vaccine. If found reliable, they could replace the use of monkeys for testing batches of the vaccine.
  5. Chemical safety testing. Also called toxicity or safety testing, this follows the same procedure as drug testing. Transgenic animals are made that carry genes making them more sensitive to toxic substances than non-transgenic animals. They are exposed to the substance and the effects are studied; toxicity testing in such animals gives results in less time.

A trap in this section: Rosie's milk contained human α-lactalbumin, not α-1-antitrypsin. The two 'alpha' proteins belong to two different sentences of NCERT and examiners deliberately test whether you have kept them apart.
sections.tip: Answer 'uses of transgenic animals' as five headed points in NCERT's order: physiology and development, disease models, biological products, vaccine safety, chemical safety testing. Each heading with its example is one mark.

sections.heading: 10.4 Ethical Issues: regulation, GEAC and the problem with patents
sections.body:
NCERT starts this section with a warning: the manipulation of living organisms by the human race cannot go on any further without regulation. Some ethical standards are needed to evaluate the morality of all human activities that might help or harm living organisms. Beyond morality, the biological consequences also matter: genetic modification of organisms can have unpredictable results when such organisms are introduced into the ecosystem. That sentence is the standard answer to 'why is there concern about releasing GMOs'.

GEAC. To deal with this, the Indian Government has set up organisations such as the Genetic Engineering Approval Committee (GEAC). Its job, in NCERT's words, is to make decisions regarding (i) the validity of GM research and (ii) the safety of introducing GM organisms for public services. Those two clauses are the two 'objectives of GEAC' asked in 2015. For your information, the body was renamed the Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee in 2010 and sits under the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change; write the NCERT expansion in the exam, and add the current name in brackets if you wish. GEAC's approval was needed, for example, before Bt cotton could be grown commercially in India in 2002.

Patents on living material. The modification and use of living organisms for public services (as food and medicine sources, for example) has also created problems with patents. There is growing public anger that companies are being granted patents for products and technologies that make use of genetic materials, plants and other biological resources that have long been identified, developed and used by farmers and indigenous people of a specific region or country. This is the seed of the biopiracy idea developed in the next section.

Two more points that can complete a 5-mark answer on biosafety and ethics. First, the Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety (2000, under the Convention on Biological Diversity) governs the international movement of living modified organisms; India is a party. Second, ethical questions about transgenic animals include the welfare of the animals themselves, and questions about gene therapy include whether changes should ever be made to the embryo (the germ line), since those would be inherited. NCERT does not detail these, so keep them to a sentence each.
sections.tip: Write GEAC's two objectives in two separate lines: validity of GM research, and safety of introducing GMOs for public services. 'To check GM crops' is too vague for two marks.

sections.heading: 10.4 Biopiracy: the Basmati case, turmeric and neem, and the Indian Patents Bill
sections.body:
The Basmati story. Rice has been grown in Asia for thousands of years, and India alone has an estimated 200,000 varieties; the diversity of rice in India is one of the richest in the world. Basmati is distinct for its unique flavour and aroma, there are 27 documented varieties of Basmati grown in India, and it appears in ancient texts, folklore and poetry. In 1997, an American company (RiceTec, though NCERT does not name it) obtained patent rights on Basmati rice through the US Patent and Trademark Office. This allowed the company to sell a 'new' variety of Basmati in the US and abroad. That 'new' variety had actually been derived from Indian farmers' varieties: Indian Basmati was crossed with semi-dwarf varieties and claimed as an invention or novelty. The patent extended to functional equivalents, which meant that other people selling Basmati rice could be restricted by it. Several attempts have also been made to patent uses, products and processes based on Indian traditional herbal medicines, for example turmeric and neem. NCERT's conclusion is a sentence you can quote: if we are not vigilant and do not immediately counter such patent applications, other countries or individuals may encash on our rich legacy and we cannot do anything about it.

Definition of biopiracy. Biopiracy is the use of bio-resources by multinational companies and other organisations without proper authorisation from the countries and people concerned and without compensatory payment. Write all three parts: who, without authorisation, without compensation.

The North–South imbalance. Most industrialised nations are rich financially but poor in biodiversity and traditional knowledge. The developing and underdeveloped world is the reverse: rich in biodiversity and in traditional knowledge related to bio-resources. Traditional knowledge can be exploited to develop modern applications and can save time, effort and expenditure during commercialisation, which is exactly why it is worth taking. There has been a growing realisation of the injustice, inadequate compensation and benefit sharing between developed and developing countries.

What has been done. Some nations are developing laws to prevent such unauthorised exploitation of their bio-resources and traditional knowledge. The Indian Parliament has cleared the second amendment of the Indian Patents Bill, which takes such issues into consideration, including patent terms, emergency provisions and research and development initiative. 'Biopiracy should be prevented; state why and how' (2011) wants the definition, the injustice to the source community, and the Patents Bill amendment as the 'how'. India's Biological Diversity Act, 2002 and the Traditional Knowledge Digital Library are further measures you can mention; the neem and turmeric patents were in fact revoked after challenges backed by Indian institutions.
sections.tip: The numbers examiners pick from this section: 1997 (Basmati patent), 27 (documented Basmati varieties), 200,000 (rice varieties in India). Do not confuse 1997 (Basmati) with 1997 (Rosie) with 1990 (gene therapy) with 1983 (Eli Lilly insulin); make a dated list and test yourself on it.

key_terms.definition: The industrial-scale production of biopharmaceuticals and biologicals using genetically modified microbes, fungi, plants and animals, applied to therapeutics, diagnostics, GM crops, processed food, bioremediation, waste treatment and energy production.
A plant, bacterium, fungus or animal whose genes have been altered by manipulation, usually by transferring one or more genes from another organism through recombinant DNA technology.

A toxic insecticidal protein produced as crystals by Bacillus thuringiensis during a particular phase of its growth; coded by cry genes and specific to insect groups such as lepidopterans, coleopterans and dipterans.
The inactive form in which the Bt toxin exists inside the bacterium; it is converted to the active toxin only when the alkaline pH of an insect's gut solubilises the crystal.
The genes of Bacillus thuringiensis that code for the crystal (Cry) proteins; cryIAc and cryIIAb control the cotton bollworm, cryIAb controls the corn borer.

ncert_questions.q: Crystals of Bt toxin produced by some bacteria do not kill the bacteria themselves because
ncert_questions.a: The toxin exists inside Bacillus thuringiensis as an inactive protoxin, packed into crystals. It becomes active only after an insect ingests it: the alkaline pH of the insect's gut solubilises the crystals and converts the protoxin into the active toxin. The bacterial cell has neither the alkaline environment nor the midgut receptors the active toxin binds to, so it is unharmed. In the insect, the activated toxin binds to the surface of the midgut epithelial cells, creates pores, causes swelling and lysis of the cells, and kills the insect.

ncert_questions.q: What are transgenic bacteria? Illustrate using any one example.
ncert_questions.a:
Transgenic bacteria are bacteria whose DNA has been manipulated to carry and express a foreign gene, so that they make a product they could not make naturally.

Example: E. coli producing human insulin. In 1983 Eli Lilly prepared two DNA sequences corresponding to chains A and B of human insulin and introduced them into plasmids of E. coli. The transformed bacteria produced the two chains separately; the chains were extracted and combined by forming disulphide bonds to give functional human insulin. Because it is the human protein, this insulin does not cause the allergic reactions that insulin from cattle and pig pancreas caused.

(Other acceptable examples: E. coli making human growth hormone; yeast, a fungus, making the hepatitis B surface antigen for the vaccine.)

ncert_questions.q: Compare and contrast the advantages and disadvantages of production of genetically modified crops.
ncert_questions.a:
Advantages (NCERT list): (1) tolerance to abiotic stresses such as cold, drought, salt and heat; (2) reduced reliance on chemical pesticides through pest-resistant crops such as Bt cotton; (3) reduced post-harvest losses; (4) more efficient use of minerals, which prevents early exhaustion of soil fertility; (5) enhanced nutritional value, for example vitamin A-enriched golden rice; (6) tailor-made plants supplying industry with starches, fuels and pharmaceuticals.

Disadvantages: (1) genetic modification can have unpredictable results when the organism is released into an ecosystem; (2) the transgene may spread to wild relatives or weeds through pollen (gene flow); (3) the new protein may be allergenic or have unknown health effects, so rigorous testing is needed; (4) pests may evolve resistance to the toxin (bollworm resistance to Cry proteins has been reported), and non-target insects may be affected; (5) dependence on a few GM varieties and on seed companies can reduce crop biodiversity and farmers' autonomy; (6) patents on GM crops and on native varieties raise issues of biopiracy and ethics.

Contrast in one line: GM crops reduce the need for agrochemicals and raise yield and nutrition, but at the cost of ecological uncertainty, possible resistance and legal or ethical disputes, which is why bodies such as GEAC must approve each release.

ncert_questions.q: What are Cry proteins? Name an organism that produces it. How does man benefit from it?
ncert_questions.a:
Cry proteins are the toxic insecticidal proteins present in the crystals formed by the bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis during a particular phase of its growth. They are coded by cry genes and exist as inactive protoxins that become active in the alkaline gut of specific insect groups (lepidopterans, coleopterans, dipterans).

Organism: Bacillus thuringiensis.

Benefit to man: Specific cry genes have been isolated and introduced into crop plants. Bt cotton carrying cryIAc and cryIIAb is protected from the cotton bollworm, and cryIAb protects corn from the corn borer. The plant makes its own insecticide, so the farmer gets a higher yield, uses much less chemical pesticide, and the toxin is specific to the target pest and harmless to humans and non-target organisms.

ncert_questions.q: What is gene therapy? Illustrate using the example of adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency.
ncert_questions.a:
Gene therapy is a collection of methods that allows correction of a gene defect diagnosed in a child or embryo. A normal gene is delivered into the individual's cells or into the embryo to take over the function of, and compensate for, the non-functional gene.

ADA deficiency example. Adenosine deaminase is an enzyme crucial for the immune system; the disorder is caused by deletion of the ADA gene. It can sometimes be cured by bone marrow transplantation, or treated by enzyme replacement therapy (functional ADA injected), but neither is completely curative.

The first clinical gene therapy was given in 1990 to a 4-year-old girl with ADA deficiency: (1) lymphocytes were taken from her blood and grown in culture outside the body; (2) a functional ADA cDNA was introduced into the lymphocytes using a retroviral vector; (3) the engineered lymphocytes were returned to the patient. (4) Because these cells are not immortal, the patient needs periodic infusion of such engineered lymphocytes. A permanent cure would be possible if the ADA gene isolated from marrow cells were introduced into cells at an early embryonic stage.

ncert_questions.q: Diagrammatically represent the experimental steps in cloning and expressing a human gene (say the gene for growth hormone) into a bacterium like E. coli.
ncert_questions.a:
Draw and label the following sequence (the diagram is described in the diagrams section):

  1. Isolation of the gene: the human growth hormone gene is obtained, usually as cDNA made from its mRNA by reverse transcriptase so that it has no introns.
  2. Cutting: the gene and a plasmid vector (with ori, an antibiotic-resistance selectable marker and a bacterial promoter) are cut with the same restriction enzyme, e.g. EcoRI, to give matching sticky ends.
  3. Ligation: DNA ligase joins the gene into the plasmid downstream of the promoter, forming the recombinant plasmid.
  4. Transformation: the recombinant plasmid is introduced into competent E. coli cells (CaCl2 treatment followed by heat shock).
  5. Selection: cells are plated on antibiotic medium; only transformants carrying the plasmid grow (insertional inactivation or a reporter can be used to pick recombinants).
  6. Expression: the selected clone is cultured in a bioreactor where the promoter drives transcription and translation of the growth hormone gene.
  7. Downstream processing: the cells are broken open, the growth hormone is separated and purified, formulated with preservatives and put through clinical trials.

ncert_questions.q: Can you suggest a method to remove oil (hydrocarbon) from seeds based on your understanding of rDNA technology and chemistry of oil?
ncert_questions.a:
Seed oil is chemically a triglyceride: one glycerol molecule esterified to three fatty acids. Its synthesis in the seed needs specific enzymes, for example acetyl-CoA carboxylase for fatty acid synthesis and diacylglycerol acyltransferase (DGAT) for the final esterification step.

Two rDNA approaches: (1) Silence the oil-synthesis genes. Introduce, through Agrobacterium, a construct that produces sense and antisense RNA of the DGAT (or acyl-transferase) gene, so that dsRNA forms and RNA interference silences the gene in the seed; the seed then stores starch and protein instead of oil. (2) Introduce a lipase gene under a seed-specific promoter, so that any triglyceride formed is hydrolysed into glycerol and fatty acids, which the seed can metabolise; the mature seed is left oil-free. Either method gives oil-free seeds without the solvent extraction used at present.

ncert_questions.q: Find out from internet what is golden rice.
ncert_questions.a:
Golden rice is a genetically modified variety of rice (Oryza sativa) engineered to make β-carotene (provitamin A) in its endosperm, which gives the grain a golden colour. Ordinary polished rice has no β-carotene in the endosperm.

It was developed by Ingo Potrykus and Peter Beyer and reported in 2000. Two genes were introduced: phytoene synthase (psy) from daffodil (later replaced by the maize gene in Golden Rice 2, which makes much more β-carotene) and phytoene desaturase (crtI) from the bacterium Erwinia uredovora, together completing the β-carotene pathway in the endosperm.

Purpose: to fight vitamin A deficiency, which causes night blindness, complete blindness and higher child mortality in rice-eating populations of Asia and Africa. NCERT cites it as its example of a GM crop with enhanced nutritional value ('vitamin A enriched rice').

ncert_questions.q: Does our blood have proteases and nucleases?
ncert_questions.a:
Yes. Blood plasma contains several proteases: the enzymes of the blood-clotting cascade (thrombin, which converts fibrinogen to fibrin, and factors such as Xa), plasmin (which dissolves clots) and the proteases of the complement system. Blood also contains nucleases such as DNase I and ribonucleases, which degrade free DNA and RNA released from dead cells or pathogens.

Their presence is one reason a protein or nucleic acid drug injected into the blood has a short life, and why the DNA used in gene therapy must be packaged in a vector (a retrovirus in the ADA case) to reach the target cells intact.

ncert_questions.q: Consult internet and find out how to make orally active protein pharmaceutical. What is the major problem to be encountered?
ncert_questions.a:
The major problem: a protein taken by mouth is treated like food. It is denatured by the acid of the stomach and digested by proteases (pepsin in the stomach; trypsin, chymotrypsin and peptidases in the intestine) into amino acids, and any intact protein that survives is too large to cross the intestinal epithelium into the blood. This is why insulin cannot be swallowed and must be injected.

Ways of making a protein orally active: (1) an enteric coating that resists stomach acid and dissolves only in the intestine; (2) encapsulation in liposomes, nanoparticles or microspheres that shield the protein from proteases; (3) co-administering protease inhibitors and absorption enhancers; (4) chemical modification of the protein (e.g. attaching polyethylene glycol, PEGylation, or altering amino acids at cleavage sites) so that proteases cannot act on it; (5) expressing the protein in an edible plant (a plant-based edible vaccine) whose cell walls protect it in the stomach. Oral insulin and oral vaccines made by these routes are under trial.

pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: PCR amplifies very small amounts of nucleic acid and is routinely used to detect HIV early; ELISA detects antigen or antibody, and autoradiography reads a hybridised probe.

pyq.answer: d
pyq.solution: NCERT: transgenic rats, rabbits, pigs, sheep, cows and fish have been produced, but over 95 per cent are mice.

options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A

pyq.q: Write the two specific cry genes that encode the proteins which control cotton bollworms. Name the organism from which they were isolated.
pyq.answer: The genes are cryIAc and cryIIAb. They were isolated from the soil bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis and incorporated into cotton to give Bt cotton. (The gene cryIAb controls the corn borer, not bollworm.)

pyq.q: Mention the chemical change that pro-insulin undergoes to be able to act as mature insulin. Why did Eli Lilly not need this step?
pyq.answer:
Pro-insulin contains an extra stretch, the C peptide, connecting chains A and B. During maturation the C peptide is removed, leaving chains A and B joined by disulphide bridges as functional insulin.

Eli Lilly produced chains A and B separately in E. coli from two synthetic DNA sequences and then joined them by creating disulphide bonds; since pro-insulin was never made, there was no C peptide to remove.

pyq.q: Suggest any two possible treatments that can be given to a patient exhibiting adenosine deaminase deficiency. Why are they not completely curative?
pyq.answer:
(i) Bone marrow transplantation, which can cure the disorder in some children. (ii) Enzyme replacement therapy, in which functional ADA is given to the patient by injection.

Neither is completely curative: a compatible donor is not always available, and the injected enzyme is used up, so the injections must be repeated periodically. Gene therapy with engineered lymphocytes is the third option, and even that needs periodic infusion unless the gene is introduced at the embryonic stage.

pyq.q: Mention two objectives of setting up GEAC by the Government of India.
pyq.answer: GEAC (Genetic Engineering Approval Committee) was set up to make decisions regarding: (i) the validity of GM research, and (ii) the safety of introducing GM organisms for public services (as food and medicine sources, for example). It is needed because genetic modification can have unpredictable results when the organism is introduced into an ecosystem.

pyq.q: How does dsRNA gain entry into a eukaryotic cell to cause RNA interference? Name the process it triggers.
pyq.answer:
The complementary dsRNA may come from (i) infection by viruses having RNA genomes, or (ii) mobile genetic elements (transposons) that replicate through an RNA intermediate. In transgenic plants it is produced deliberately by introducing a gene that makes both sense and antisense RNA.

It triggers RNA interference (RNAi), in which the dsRNA binds a specific mRNA and prevents its translation (silencing); this is a method of cellular defence in all eukaryotes.

pyq.q: What is biopiracy? Name two Indian traditional products whose uses were subjected to patent attempts.
pyq.answer:
Biopiracy is the use of bio-resources by multinational companies and other organisations without proper authorisation from the countries and people concerned and without compensatory payment.

Attempts were made to patent uses, products and processes based on turmeric and neem; and in 1997 an American company obtained a patent on Basmati rice derived from Indian farmers' varieties.

pyq.q: Why do lepidopterans die when they feed on a Bt cotton plant? Explain how it happens.
pyq.answer:
Bt cotton carries a cry gene (cryIAc or cryIIAb) from Bacillus thuringiensis, so the plant makes the crystal (Cry) protein in its own tissues. The sequence of events when a lepidopteran larva (bollworm) feeds on it:

  1. The larva ingests the crystal protein, which is an inactive protoxin.
  2. The alkaline pH of the insect gut solubilises the crystal and converts the protoxin into the active toxin.
  3. The activated toxin binds to the surface of the midgut epithelial cells.
  4. It creates pores in the cell membranes, causing the cells to swell and lyse.
  5. The gut is destroyed, the larva stops feeding and dies.

Insects without an alkaline gut and the specific receptors are unaffected, which is why the toxin is insect-group specific and harmless to humans.

pyq.q: How has the use of Agrobacterium as a vector helped in controlling Meloidogyne incognita infestation in tobacco plants? Explain in correct sequence.
pyq.answer:
1. Meloidogyne incognita is a nematode that infects the roots of tobacco and reduces yield.
  2. Using Agrobacterium vectors, nematode-specific genes were introduced into the tobacco plant.
  3. The DNA was introduced so that the plant cells produced both sense and antisense RNA.
  4. The two complementary RNAs paired to form double-stranded RNA (dsRNA).
  5. The dsRNA initiated RNA interference and silenced the specific mRNA of the nematode, blocking its translation.
  6. Unable to make the essential protein, the parasite could not survive in the transgenic host, so the plant protected itself.

pyq.q: Explain the various steps involved in the production of genetically engineered insulin. How does it differ from the insulin produced by the human pancreas?
pyq.answer:
Steps (Eli Lilly, 1983): (1) Two DNA sequences corresponding to the A and B chains of human insulin were prepared. (2) Each was introduced into a plasmid of E. coli. (3) The transformed bacteria produced chains A and B separately. (4) The chains were extracted and purified. (5) They were combined by creating disulphide bonds to form functional human insulin.

Difference: The human pancreas synthesises insulin as a pro-hormone (pro-insulin) containing an extra C peptide that joins chains A and B and is removed during maturation. Recombinant insulin is assembled directly from separately made A and B chains, so no C peptide is ever formed and no maturation step is needed. The final product is otherwise identical to human insulin and, unlike cattle or pig insulin, causes no allergic reaction.

pyq.q: Why is molecular diagnosis preferred over conventional methods? Name any two molecular techniques, giving one use of each.
pyq.answer:
Why preferred: Effective treatment needs early diagnosis. With conventional methods (serum and urine analysis) a pathogen is suspected only after it has produced symptoms, when its concentration in the body is already very high. Molecular techniques detect the pathogen or the defective gene at very low concentration, before symptoms appear.

Techniques: (i) PCR: amplifies the nucleic acid of a pathogen and is used to detect HIV in suspected AIDS patients and mutations in genes of suspected cancer patients. (ii) ELISA: based on antigen–antibody interaction; detects infection by the presence of the pathogen's antigens or of antibodies made against it. (A radioactive DNA probe with autoradiography, which shows that a mutant clone does not hybridise, is a third acceptable technique.)

pyq.q: Explain enzyme replacement therapy to treat adenosine deaminase deficiency. Mention two disadvantages of this procedure and suggest a better alternative.
pyq.answer:
Enzyme replacement therapy: ADA deficiency is caused by deletion of the gene for adenosine deaminase, an enzyme crucial for the immune system. In ERT, functional ADA enzyme is given to the patient by injection to make up for the missing enzyme.

Disadvantages: (i) it is not completely curative, because the defect in the gene remains; (ii) the enzyme is used up, so the patient needs periodic injections for life.

Better alternative: gene therapy: the patient's lymphocytes are cultured, a functional ADA cDNA is introduced with a retroviral vector, and the cells are returned; a permanent cure is possible if the gene is introduced into cells at an early embryonic stage.

pyq.q: What is a GMO? List any four possible advantages of a GM crop to a farmer.
pyq.answer:
A genetically modified organism (GMO) is a plant, bacterium, fungus or animal whose genes have been altered by manipulation, usually by introducing a gene from another organism by recombinant DNA technology.

Advantages to the farmer: (i) crops tolerant to abiotic stresses such as cold, drought, salt and heat, so they survive bad seasons; (ii) pest-resistant crops such as Bt cotton, which reduce the cost of and reliance on chemical pesticides; (iii) reduced post-harvest losses; (iv) more efficient use of minerals, which prevents early exhaustion of soil fertility and lowers fertiliser cost; (v) enhanced nutritional value, as in golden rice, which fetches a better product.

pyq.q: Explain the application of biotechnology in producing Bt cotton. Why does the Bt toxin not kill the bacterium that produces it, but kills the insect that ingests it?
pyq.answer:
Source of the toxin. The soil bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) forms protein crystals during a particular phase of its growth. The crystals contain a toxic insecticidal protein (Cry protein) that kills certain insects: lepidopterans (tobacco budworm, armyworm), coleopterans (beetles) and dipterans (flies, mosquitoes).

Making Bt cotton. Specific Bt toxin genes, called cry genes, were isolated from B. thuringiensis and incorporated into cotton using rDNA technology. The choice of gene depends on the crop and the target pest, because most Bt toxins are insect-group specific: the proteins coded by cryIAc and cryIIAb control the cotton bollworm, and cryIAb controls the corn borer. The transgenic cotton plant expresses the cry gene and makes the Cry protein in its tissues, so bollworm larvae feeding on it die and the crop needs far less chemical insecticide.

Why the bacterium survives. Inside the bacterium the toxin exists as an inactive protoxin packed in crystals; the bacterium has neither the alkaline environment to activate it nor the gut receptors it acts on.

Why the insect dies. When the insect ingests the crystal, the alkaline pH of its gut solubilises the crystal and converts the protoxin into the active toxin. The active toxin binds to the surface of the midgut epithelial cells and creates pores, the cells swell and lyse, the gut is destroyed and the insect dies.

(Draw the flow chart: crystal protoxin → ingestion → alkaline gut → active toxin → binding to midgut epithelium → pores → lysis → death.)

pyq.q: (i) Name the source from which insulin was extracted earlier. Why is this insulin no longer used by diabetic people? (ii) Explain the process of synthesis of insulin by the Eli Lilly company and name the technique used. (iii) How is the insulin produced by the human body different from the insulin produced by the company?
pyq.answer:
(i) Insulin was earlier extracted from the pancreas of slaughtered cattle and pigs. It is no longer used because it is a foreign protein: some patients developed allergy or other reactions to it. Recombinant human insulin causes no such reaction.

(ii) Technique: recombinant DNA technology. In 1983 Eli Lilly prepared two DNA sequences corresponding to chains A and B of human insulin and introduced them into plasmids of E. coli. The transformed bacteria produced the two chains separately. The chains were extracted and then combined by creating disulphide bonds between them to form human insulin.

(iii) In the human body insulin is synthesised as a pro-hormone, pro-insulin, which contains chains A and B plus an extra stretch, the C peptide; the C peptide is removed during maturation to give functional insulin. The company's insulin is assembled directly from separately made A and B chains, so it never contains a C peptide and needs no maturation step. The main challenge of the rDNA method was precisely this: getting insulin assembled into its mature two-chain form, which Eli Lilly solved by making the chains separately.

pyq.q: (i) What are transgenic animals? (ii) Name the transgenic animal that has the largest number among all existing transgenic animals. (iii) Explain any three purposes for which transgenic animals are produced, with one example each.
pyq.answer:
(i) Transgenic animals are animals that have had their DNA manipulated to possess and express an extra (foreign) gene. Transgenic rats, rabbits, pigs, sheep, cows and fish have been produced.

(ii) Mice: over 95 per cent of all existing transgenic animals are mice.

(iii) Purposes (any three):

  1. Normal physiology and development: to study how genes are regulated and how they affect normal body function and development, e.g. introducing genes that alter the formation of insulin-like growth factor and studying its biological effects.
  2. Study of disease: transgenic animals serve as models for human diseases so that new treatments can be tested; models exist for cancer, cystic fibrosis, rheumatoid arthritis and Alzheimer's disease.
  3. Biological products: animals carrying the gene for a human protein produce it cheaply, e.g. α-1-antitrypsin used to treat emphysema; the first transgenic cow, Rosie (1997), gave milk containing 2.4 g/L of human α-lactalbumin, more balanced for human babies than cow milk.
  4. Vaccine safety: transgenic mice are used to test the safety of the polio vaccine before human use, and may replace monkeys for this.
  5. Chemical safety testing: transgenic animals carrying genes that make them more sensitive to toxic substances give toxicity results in less time.

pyq.q: What is gene therapy? Describe, in sequence, how the first clinical gene therapy was carried out. Why was it not a permanent cure, and what could make it permanent?
pyq.answer:
Gene therapy is a collection of methods that allows correction of a gene defect diagnosed in a child or embryo: a normal gene is delivered into the individual's cells or into the embryo to take over the function of, and compensate for, the non-functional gene.

The first clinical gene therapy (1990) was given to a 4-year-old girl with adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency, caused by deletion of the ADA gene; the enzyme is crucial for the immune system.

  1. Lymphocytes from the patient's blood were grown in culture outside the body.
  2. A functional ADA cDNA was introduced into these lymphocytes using a retroviral vector.
  3. The genetically engineered lymphocytes were returned to the patient, where they produced ADA.

Why not permanent: the engineered lymphocytes are not immortal; they die after their normal life span, so the patient needs periodic infusion of such cells.

Permanent cure: if the ADA gene isolated from marrow cells producing ADA is introduced into cells at an early embryonic stage, all cells of the body, including the stem cells that keep making lymphocytes, would carry the working gene, and the cure would be permanent. Conventional alternatives, bone marrow transplantation and enzyme replacement therapy, are not completely curative either.

pyq.q:
Read the passage and answer the questions. A farmer in Maharashtra switched from conventional cotton to Bt cotton after losing most of his crop to bollworm for two seasons. The Bt seed carries genes isolated from a soil bacterium, and the plant now makes a crystal protein in its own tissues. His neighbour worries that the protein will poison people who wear cotton or the birds that eat the insects.
(i) Name the bacterium and the two genes that make the cotton resistant to bollworm.
(ii) Why does the crystal protein not harm the bacterium that produces it?
(iii) Explain in two lines how the protein kills the bollworm larva.
(iv) Give one reason the neighbour's worry about people and birds is unfounded.
pyq.answer:
(i) Bacillus thuringiensis; the genes are cryIAc and cryIIAb.

(ii) Inside the bacterium the toxin exists as an inactive protoxin in the crystal; it is activated only by the alkaline pH of an insect gut, which the bacterium does not have.

(iii) In the larva's alkaline gut the protoxin is converted to the active toxin, which binds to the midgut epithelial cells, creates pores, and causes the cells to swell and lyse, killing the larva.

(iv) Bt toxins are insect-group specific: they act only on cells with an alkaline gut and the specific receptors (lepidopterans, coleopterans, dipterans). Humans and birds have an acidic stomach and no such receptors, so the protein is simply digested like any other protein.

pyq.q:
Read the passage and answer the questions. A four-year-old child has repeated severe infections. Tests show that her lymphocytes lack an enzyme needed for the immune system, because the gene coding for it has been deleted. A bone marrow donor cannot be found. Doctors first inject the enzyme, and later offer a newer treatment in which some of her own blood cells are taken, modified in the laboratory and returned to her.
(i) Name the enzyme and the disorder.
(ii) What is the name of the treatment by injection, and what is its limitation?
(iii) Name the cells that are taken from the child, the vector used to modify them and the DNA introduced.
(iv) Why will she need the modified cells again and again, and what could give her a permanent cure?
pyq.answer:
(i) The enzyme is adenosine deaminase (ADA); the disorder is ADA deficiency, a severe immunodeficiency caused by deletion of the ADA gene.

(ii) Enzyme replacement therapy: functional ADA is given by injection. It is not completely curative; the enzyme is used up and the injections must be repeated periodically.

(iii) Lymphocytes from her blood are grown in culture; a functional ADA cDNA is introduced into them using a retroviral vector; the engineered lymphocytes are then returned to her. This was the first clinical gene therapy, given in 1990.

(iv) The engineered lymphocytes are not immortal, so as they die the corrected gene is lost and she needs periodic infusion of fresh engineered cells. A permanent cure would be possible if the ADA gene isolated from marrow cells were introduced into her cells at an early embryonic stage, so that every cell, including the stem cells that produce lymphocytes, carried it.

common_mistakes: Writing cryIAb for the cotton bollworm. The bollworm genes are cryIAc and cryIIAb; cryIAb controls the corn borer. A single wrong letter loses the mark.

Saying the Bt toxin is 'secreted' or 'active' in the bacterium. It is an inactive protoxin in a crystal; it is activated only by the alkaline pH of the insect gut. Answers that skip 'protoxin' and 'alkaline' lose the reasoning marks.

Naming the wrong vector. Agrobacterium carried the nematode-specific genes into tobacco; a retrovirus carried the ADA cDNA into lymphocytes; E. coli plasmids carried the insulin chain genes. Students swap these under pressure.

Describing RNAi as something that stops transcription or destroys DNA. NCERT's RNAi silences a specific mRNA because a complementary dsRNA binds it and prevents translation. Also, both sense and antisense RNA must be mentioned, since the dsRNA forms from them.

Confusing the C peptide with chain C. Pro-insulin has chains A and B plus a connecting C peptide that is removed on maturation; Eli Lilly made A and B separately and never made a C peptide. Answers that say 'Eli Lilly removed the C peptide' are wrong.

Writing that gene therapy for ADA was a permanent cure. The engineered lymphocytes are not immortal, so periodic infusion is needed; the permanent cure is a suggestion, introducing the gene at the embryonic stage, not what was done in 1990.
Mixing up Rosie's α-lactalbumin with α-1-antitrypsin. Rosie's milk had 2.4 g/L human α-lactalbumin; α-1-antitrypsin is the transgenic product used for emphysema.

Giving a vague definition of biopiracy. All three parts are needed: use of bio-resources by multinational companies or other organisations, without proper authorisation from the countries and people concerned, and without compensatory payment.
Confusing the dates. 1983 Eli Lilly insulin, 1990 first gene therapy, 1997 Rosie and also 1997 the Basmati patent. Make a dated list and revise it the night before.

Answering 'why molecular diagnosis' with 'it is more accurate'. The NCERT reason is early detection: conventional methods detect a pathogen only after symptoms, when its numbers are high, while PCR detects very low concentrations before symptoms appear.
strategy:
This is a short chapter with five stories and one list of ethics, so prepare it as stories, not as scattered facts. Write out, from memory and in sequence, (1) Bt cotton from the bacterium to the dead bollworm, (2) RNAi from Agrobacterium to the dead nematode, (3) insulin from the slaughtered pig to Eli Lilly's disulphide bonds, (4) gene therapy from the deleted ADA gene to the periodic infusion, and (5) the five uses of transgenic animals. Each story should take you under three minutes to write; if it takes longer, you are adding padding the marking scheme does not reward.

Memorise the names and numbers as a single sheet: cryIAc, cryIIAb, cryIAb; Meloidogyne incognita, tobacco, Agrobacterium; 1983, chains A and B, C peptide, E. coli; 1990, 4-year-old girl, lymphocytes, retroviral vector, ADA cDNA; PCR, probe, autoradiography, ELISA; 95 per cent mice, α-1-antitrypsin, Rosie 1997, 2.4 g/L α-lactalbumin, polio vaccine; GEAC, 1997 Basmati, 27 varieties, 200,000 varieties, turmeric, neem, second amendment of the Patents Bill. Test yourself on this sheet on three separate days.

Practise the flow charts for Bt toxin action, RNAi and gene therapy, and the pro-insulin figure; a labelled flow chart is the fastest way to secure a 5-mark question and is accepted by CBSE marking schemes in place of prose. Spend ten minutes on the GM crop advantage list and the three critical research areas, both of which are copied straight from NCERT in the marking scheme.

In the exam, expect one or two 1-mark items and one 3- or 5-mark question from this chapter. Give the 1-mark items ten seconds each (they are pure recall) and reserve six to eight minutes for the long question, writing in numbered steps with the NCERT keywords underlined.
